thread.title: ProSnap, GoFace, Or iGo Coming Soon? - GoPro (NASDAQ:GPRO)

author: Robert Leonard
title: ProSnap, GoFace, Or iGo Coming Soon? - GoPro (NASDAQ:GPRO)
text:
There's long been speculation that GoPro ( GPRO ) would be acquired, but have recent actions by GoPro provided an indication that a sale could be coming sooner rather than later? It recently released the 'GoPro Hero', a cheaper camera priced to attract the attention of a wider audience while still having many of the best features from the far more expensive Hero 5 and Hero 6 models. GoPro Founder and CEO Nick Woodman also stated , "We're 'absolutely' open to selling company." Woodman has even started discussions with JP Morgan to advise a sale of the GoPro. GoPro is down more than 92% since its all-time high, making it a much more affordable (and reasonable) acquisition target.
GPRO data by YCharts
I initially became interested in the idea of GoPro being acquired after reading Aditya Agashe's intriguing post on LinkedIn stating, "Prediction: Snap Inc. will acquire GoPro by the end of 2019."
His post got me thinking; does Snap Inc. ( SNAP ) acquiring GoPro make sense, is it possible, and would it be the most successful buyer? I concluded it does make sense, and they have the resources to do so, but I am not convinced they would be the most successful buyer. Other companies such as Facebook Inc. ( FB ), Apple Inc. ( AAPL ), Garmin Ltd. ( GRMN ), Xiaomi ( XI ), Alphabet Inc. ( GOOG ), Amazon ( AMZN ), and Sony ( SNE ) all possess the necessary resources to make the acquisition and each has interesting characteristics that could make it an intriguing acquisition.
Avoiding A Competitive Battle Snap acquiring GoPro has long been the most coveted scenario by mainstream financial media. It seems GoPro wants to be Snap, and Snap wants to be GoPro, making an acquisition a plausible outcome. Woodman has publicly discussed GoPro attempting to become a 'storytelling' company, with its cameras providing one point in that storytelling solution. Originally GoPro was a camera company, but the recent change of heart by Woodman shows the company moving in a different direction.
Everyone thought Snap was built as a 'storytelling' (or social media) company through its app Snapchat. Its Stories feature provides users with a storytelling platform that can be used to broadcast their story for all to see. Snapchat users can also share their stories directly with other Snapchat users. With its flagship product being based on storytelling, many people were caught off guard when Snap proclaimed it is a camera company.
It seems somewhat "silly", but GoPro is attempting to do what Snap is good at, software and services, while Snap is attempting to do what GoPro is good at, hardware/cameras. GoPro is focusing on allowing users to transfer videos to the cloud, their cellphones, and other devices immediately and seamlessly for a better user experience. GoPro cameras can be connected to a user's iPhone via WiFi and then live streamed through Periscope, a live streaming service. This has been popular with GoPro users with the increasing popularity of live streaming. On the other side, Snap is trying to make hardware work (for the second time). It has recently released its second version of its sunglasses camera, Spectacles. Although slightly better than the first release, the second release of Spectacles was not very successful; neither release of the Spectacles have been all that popular or successful for Snap.
Combining GoPro and Snap could prove they are stronger together than they are on their own by providing a solution to both company's problems. GoPro can help with Snap's hardware, Snap can help with GoPro's software and services. Not to mention, it would save the two companies from having to compete head-to-head.
Facebook Acquiring GoPro May Not Be As Farfetched As It Seems on the Surface Facebook has been very successfully operating its high-margin social media platform, why would it ever want to get into lower margin hardware products like GoPro's cameras? The argument for Facebook itself isn't as strong as it is for some of the entities Facebook owns, like Instagram. One of the interesting options for Facebook itself is that it could integrate the cameras into its rapidly growing Facebook Live feature to increase participation and returning users to the platform as a whole.
However, a more interesting opportunity exists with Instagram. Remember, Facebook tried to buy Snap , but the offer was declined. Ever since then, Mark Zuckerberg has been trying to crush Snap. Facebook's main platform, and subsidiary Instagram, have emulated some of Snap's most popular features, such as Stories, with great success. Zuckerberg could use GoPro in an attempt to crush Snap's Spectacles and other hardware/camera projects Snap has planned. He was willing to spend $3 billion to stop users from flocking to Snapchat from Facebook; it's certainly reasonable he'd spend about $980 million to stop Snap's success with Spectacles and other hardware products. Facebook could also use the GoPro cameras, the technology, its supply chain expertise, or camera development expertise in its subsidiary Oculus VR. Although less likely, Facebook may also be able to integrate a GoPro-like camera into WhatsApp or Facebook Messenger.
Apple Doesn't Really Need GoPro, But It Didn't Need Beats, Either Apple's relationship and actions towards GoPro have been interesting. Reportedly, back in 2015 Apple patented a wearable camera similar to GoPro's, but better. Apple's 34 patents are based on improving significantly on GoPro's weaknesses and flaws. Not much has come from this as of yet, but Apple does focus heavily on their cameras each time a new iPhone is released. Apple has dominated many, if not all, of the markets it participates in and needs to find new avenues for growth as it nears a $1 trillion market cap. Could a durable external camera that can be controlled with an iPhone be part of that solution? The market for these cameras is not nearly as large as its other markets, but it could make for an interesting new segment with not much effort or investment. Other integration with Apple Watches could make for another interesting use of GoPro cameras, technology, or expertise. Bringing some of Apple's strengths, such as chip producing, cellular technology, and computing power, to a GoPro camera could greatly improve its prospects. Apple's cloud software and tools would also align very well with Woodman's future vision for GoPro. Apple also has famously been successful at selling "overpriced" products, which many customers complain GoPro cameras are. With the patents Apple has, it doesn't really need GoPro, but it also didn't really need Beats either, yet it paid about $3 billion to acquire it. Plus, Apple has a plethora of cash. At just under $1 billion, GoPro wouldn't even make a dent in Apple's cash holdings. Adding an Apple-improved GoPro camera to the Apple ecosystem could be interesting.
A GoPro Smartphone? Anyone who has used Alphabet's Google Pixel 2 knows just how good the camera is. So, it's safe to say Alphabet doesn't need much help in that realm, but where Alphabet, Amazon, Sony, or Xiaomi may be able to use the cameras is in producing a rugged smartphone with a high quality camera. There has been speculation this is possible if one of these companies were to acquire GoPro.
Source: TechBlog
As of now, users have to have two separate devices for a durable camera and smartphone capabilities. Smartphone cameras have come a long way and can rival GoPro's quality, but they're fragile - very fragile. Combining GoPro's durability with Alphabet, Amazon, Sony, or Xiaomi's smartphone technology could provide a very interesting product to a niche market of consumers.
Xiaomi could also improve its own camera through the integration of a GoPro designed camera. Other Chinese cellphone manufacturers install other high quality cameras into their devices; Xiaomi could follow suit with GoPro.
Alphabet Has A History of Wearable Technology Alphabet has a history with wearable technology from their Google Glass products, and they have reportedly made an offer to purchase Snap for about $30 billion (Snap says this was just a rumor). This unconfirmed offer could have been, and likely was, in hopes of obtaining Snaps social media platform. However, it could also be in hopes of obtaining Snap's Spectacles to improve upon future Google Glass-type products. Combining Google-improved Snap Spectacles with GoPro technology/cameras could create an interesting product for Alphabet.
Source: TechCrunch
Combination of Two Action Sports Companies Garmin is well-known for action sports and outdoor related products, but not too long ago they released an action camera to directly compete with GoPro. Rather than competing head-to-head, the two companies may be stronger by coming together as one. Combining Garmin's outdoor/fitness products with GoPro's cameras would create an ecosystem of products that work very well together and attract both of the companies' target market - active customers. There could also be operational synergies from back-office tasks to R&D. Both companies have been struggling and the competition makes them both weaker. Coming together for the greater good could prove to create a much stronger single company.
The Bottom Line There are many, many scenarios that could play out over the ensuing months. Realistically, an acquisition of GoPro would take minimal resources from any of the companies discussed here. GoPro looks very cheap on the surface, but many analysts believe GoPro has further to fall due to its expected struggles, causing many of these companies to delay on making an acquisition bid. By waiting to make an acquisition bid, a company may be able to buy the company at an even lower price. Some companies discussed here have investments in other companies that compete with GoPro in some aspects, others may not want to weigh down their earnings with GoPro's unprofitable business, or they may just prefer to develop similar products themselves. There certainly are reasons the companies discussed in this article may not acquire GoPro, but there are also very intriguing arguments for each company to acquire it. With " GoPRO entertaining acquisition offers ", other comments by Woodman , the business failing, and its stock off all-time highs by more than 92%, I expect that an acquisition from some company at some time in the future is almost certain, but the details of the offer and who will be the acquirer is far from certain. Investors should not buy GoPro solely based on the potential of an acquisition as it could still be a long time before an acquisition is agreed to (if an acquisition materializes at all), and the terms of the acquisition could be unfavorable for shareholders.
